question.text: Ashoka Cat II AIF has a small investment team and outsources its back-office. The Manager appoints an 'Operating Manager' (sometimes called a Chief Operating Officer or Head of Fund Operations) who coordinates between the custodian, RTA, fund administrator, auditor and valuer. Which statement BEST describes the Operating Manager's role from the ecosystem-governance standpoint?

answer.text: Single-point coordinator across service providers — escalation owner for breaks, reconciliations, NAV sign-offs, PPM-audit liaison and LPAC operational updates — NOT a SEBI-registered role but critical for integrated ecosystem governance.
SEBI-registered intermediary with a separate fit-and-proper test distinct from the Manager entity.
Equivalent to the Trustee and can override IC decisions.
Replaces the Compliance Officer and Chief Investment Officer when appointed.

explanation.text: The Logic: The Operating Manager / Head of Fund Operations is the single-point coordinator across custodian, RTA, FA, valuer and auditor — owning the monthly reconciliation cycle, NAV sign-off workflow, PPM-audit liaison and LPAC operational papers. It is NOT a separately registered SEBI role (like CIO or Compliance Officer, which are Manager-entity roles), but it is central to integrated ecosystem governance. The Trap: Option B invents a separate SEBI registration. Option C confuses the role with the Trustee's governance powers. Option D wrongly claims the role absorbs CIO/CO responsibilities. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) has a similar role under the CFO/COO designation but with lighter service-provider coordination. Mutual-fund exams (V-A) assign the role to a dedicated Operations head at AMC. Manager's Pro-Tip: Your Operating Manager should own the service-provider KPI scorecard — NAV timeliness, trade settlement fails, audit observations, LP query turnaround. Review these at every quarterly IC — service-provider performance drifts quietly till a crisis surfaces.
